tables.title: Flattening can survive without an indirect jump
tables.subtitle: FLA = control-flow flattening. Look for state-driven dispatch, not one opcode.
rows: Repeated state tests and returns to dispatch.

O1: direct network
O2 and /Ox: indirect table

tables.takeaway: A direct chain of comparisons can implement the same flattened state machine as a jump table.
tables.note: Scope: demo_flattening. Survival of obfuscation does not establish compatibility with an unflattener.

tables.title: What does each deobfuscator actually produce?
tables.subtitle: Expression recovery, a branch proof, LLVM IR and a rewritten PE are different outputs.
rows: No rewritten PE in this study.
Partial reduction is not full recovery.
A produced PE can have wrong semantics.
Analysis itself does not patch the PE.
Predicates and dead bytes can remain.
tables.takeaway: Ask two questions: what representation was recovered, and how was its correctness checked?
tables.note: PE = Windows Portable Executable. The Mergen test harness is not a rewritten original PE.

tables.title: From obfuscated code to a working rewrite
tables.subtitle: All eight inputs below are runnable originals; the output claims differ sharply.
rows: msynth recovery is not binary rewriting.
Substantial MBA remains in lifted IR.
Predicates and dead clone bytes remain.
Graph need not match clean exactly.
O0 success does not extend to O2 here.
tables.takeaway: A semantic result is not automatically a working executable, and a valid PE is not automatically correct.
tables.note: PASS refers to retained validation. Successor-pair scores are not universal proofs of program equivalence.

tables.title: BCF: proof becomes a working PE patch
tables.subtitle: The same generic proof-and-patch workflow worked across two implementations.
tables.takeaway: JNE becomes JMP + NOP. Reachable flow shrinks; predicate arithmetic and dead bytes stay in the PE.
tables.note: A triple compares clean/original/rewrite. Dedicated PE CFG audit: calls do not split blocks; RET is terminal.
